However, when using the Ag-PMMA as part of an encapsulant for PSCs, it is essential to have a balanced lamination process that ensures sufficient microsphere protrusions without excessive reduction in polymer thickness (i.e., bond-line thickness). To gain a deeper understanding and to achieve better control over the relationship between lamination pressure, bond-line thickness, and out-of-plane electrical conductivity, we developed a preliminary in-house analytical model.149,150 This framework provided an approximate range of optimal lamination pressures, as we demonstrate next, which was then validated by measuring the electrical conductivities of corresponding FS-TCCs. For this study, the microsphere mechanical property was approximated as that of polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) due to negligible contributions of the thin silver membrane (<250nm) compared to the PMMA core (approx. 50µm) at room temperature. A schematic representation of the single- sphere analytical solution is shown in Figure 16a. The single-sphere model was applied to the total population of microspheres using computational methods (i.e., python). A schematic illustrating the multi-sphere model is shown in Figure 16b. In short, the multi- sphere model sums the compressive force of each microsphere under compression (i.e., single-sphere model) to predict the total compressive force required to reach a target bond-line thickness (Figure 16c), as related to the percent of microspheres in contact. Successful lamination requires sufficient microspheres to protrude slightly out of the polymer matrix without reducing the polymer thickness excessively, as illustrated in Figure 17a and b. The analytical solution was employed under these assumptions and tested for validity in-house via out-of-plane conductivity measurements. Note that lower microsphere concentrations likely required a higher degree of reduction in bond line thickness to account for the small number of microspheres per unit area. Our team is developing a comprehensive model, and the results will be published soon.
